g.text: Large language models increasingly face inputs that exceed a single context
window, such as long reports, codebases, or extensive retrieved documents.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Large language models increasingly face inputs that exceed a single context window, such as long reports, codebases, or extensive retrieved documents.

g.text: Memory agents address this by processing documents chunk-by-chunk
while maintaining a bounded working memory, enabling inference on
extremely long contexts (hundreds of thousands of tokens) at cost
g.title: N2 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Memory agents address this by processing documents chunk-by-chunk while maintaining a bounded working memory, enabling inference on extremely long contexts (hundreds of thousands of tokens) at cost proportional to document length (Yu et al., 2025).

g.text: However, this chunk-scanning approach remains computationally
expensive: processing a single query may require hundreds of
g.title: N3 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, this chunk-scanning approach remains computationally expensive: processing a single query may require hundreds of sequential memory updates.

g.text: Early stopping—terminating processing once sufficient evidence has
been gathered—offers a natural path to efficiency, with learned
stopping policies achieving 3–5× speedup (Wang et al., 2026b).
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Early stopping—terminating processing once sufficient evidence has been gathered—offers a natural path to efficiency, with learned stopping policies achieving 3–5× speedup (Wang et al., 2026b).

g.text: Learned stopping needs supervision, no safety guarantee
Yet learned stopping policies require training-time supervision
and leave deployment knobs (e.g., how aggressively to stop)
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=0) Yet learned stopping policies require training-time supervision and leave deployment knobs (e.g., how aggressively to stop) without explicit safety guarantees.

g.text: A practical deployment question remains: how do we stop early while
guaranteeing we do not break more than an ε fraction of the full-read
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) A practical deployment question remains: how do we stop early while guaranteeing we do not break more than an ε fraction of the full-read system's correct answers?

g.text: This motivates a post-hoc, training-free calibration approach that can be
applied to any existing memory agent with a user-chosen risk budget.
g.title: N7 [Method] (cites=0) This motivates a post-hoc, training-free calibration approach that can be applied to any existing memory agent with a user-chosen risk budget.

g.text: We propose RC-MemStop, which applies conformal risk control (Angelopoulos et
al., 2025) to calibrate early stopping thresholds for memory agents.
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=1) We propose RC-MemStop, which applies conformal risk control (Angelopoulos et al., 2025) to calibrate early stopping thresholds for memory agents.

g.text: RC-MemStop uses an answer-stability stopping rule: processing terminates
when k consecutive draft answers match.
g.title: N9 [Method: component] (cites=0) RC-MemStop uses an answer-stability stopping rule: processing terminates when k consecutive draft answers match.

g.text: Using the Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting bound, we select the least
conservative k that satisfies a user-specified broken-success risk budget ε
g.title: N10 [Method: component] (cites=0) Using the Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting bound, we select the least conservative k that satisfies a user-specified broken-success risk budget ε with high probability.

g.text: This approach requires no retraining and provides finite-sample guarantees
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) This approach requires no retraining and provides finite-sample guarantees on held-out test data.

g.text: Our experiments on MemAgent with 448K–896K token contexts reveal a
surprising finding: risk control is achieved, but speedup is negligible.
g.title: N12 [Result] (cites=0) Our experiments on MemAgent with 448K–896K token contexts reveal a surprising finding: risk control is achieved, but speedup is negligible.

g.text: Across all 8 configurations, we observe zero risk violations (Rtest ≤ ε),
validating that conformal risk control can be successfully applied to memory
g.title: N13 [Result] (cites=0) Across all 8 configurations, we observe zero risk violations (Rtest ≤ ε), validating that conformal risk control can be successfully applied to memory agent early stopping.

g.text: However, the best speedup is only 1.14×, far below the 1.5× target and even
g.title: N14 [Result] (cites=0) However, the best speedup is only 1.14×, far below the 1.5× target and even below the 1.2× practical utility threshold.

g.text: Root cause: stability signal too weak
The root cause is that the answer-stability signal is too weak: draft
answers do not stabilize until the agent has processed most of the context,
requiring k = 60–120 consecutive matches to control risk.
g.title: N15 [Result] (cites=0) The root cause is that the answer-stability signal is too weak: draft answers do not stabilize until the agent has processed most of the context, requiring k = 60–120 consecutive matches to control risk.

g.text: First conformal risk control for memory stopping
We present the first application of conformal risk control to
memory agent early stopping, demonstrating that UCB-calibrated
thresholds can maintain user-specified risk budgets on held-out
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We present the first application of conformal risk control to memory agent early stopping, demonstrating that UCB-calibrated thresholds can maintain user-specified risk budgets on held-out test data.

g.text: We provide empirical evidence that calibration-only early stopping
with answer stability is insufficient for meaningful compute
reduction in memory agents, achieving only 1.02×–1.14× speedup.
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We provide empirical evidence that calibration-only early stopping with answer stability is insufficient for meaningful compute reduction in memory agents, achieving only 1.02×–1.14× speedup.

g.text: Diagnosis: stability signal too weak; need training
We diagnose the root cause: the answer-stability stopping signal
is fundamentally too weak, with broken-success risk remaining
above 50% until k = 30–50 consecutive matches, suggesting that
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We diagnose the root cause: the answer-stability stopping signal is fundamentally too weak, with broken-success risk remaining above 50% until k = 30–50 consecutive matches, suggesting that training-based stopping policies are necessary for practical efficiency gains.
